subsystems.name: Emitter array
subsystems.role: produces red and near-infrared light at specific wavelengths that penetrate tissue.
parts: LEDs (typically 630–670 nm red and 810–850 nm near-infrared)

subsystems.name: Driver electronics
subsystems.role: supplies a stable, controlled current so light output stays constant.

subsystems.name: Thermal management
subsystems.role: removes heat from LEDs, which lose efficiency and shift wavelength if they overheat.

subsystems.name: Optical window
subsystems.role: spreads light evenly over the treatment area and protects the emitters.

subsystems.name: Housing and controls
subsystems.role: contains the device and lets the user set time, intensity and pulse settings.

subsystems.name: Power supply
subsystems.role: converts mains or battery power to the low-voltage DC the LEDs need.

buildSteps.title: Choose wavelengths and dose
buildSteps.detail: Select LED wavelengths based on research into how deep light penetrates and how tissue absorbs it, then set a target irradiance (power per area) and treatment time.

buildSteps.title: Mount the LEDs
buildSteps.detail: Solder or reflow LEDs onto a circuit board, often with an aluminium backing to conduct heat away.

buildSteps.title: Build the driver
buildSteps.detail: Assemble a constant-current driver and microcontroller so each LED receives the same current and can be pulsed or dimmed reliably.

buildSteps.title: Attach cooling
buildSteps.detail: Bond the board to a heat sink and fit a fan or vents so the panel can run for many minutes without overheating.

buildSteps.title: Fit the optical window
buildSteps.detail: Place a diffuser over the LEDs to blur bright spots and spread light evenly across the skin.

buildSteps.title: Enclose and wire controls
buildSteps.detail: Install the board, driver and power supply in the housing, connect the timer and buttons, and seal the unit.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate and test
buildSteps.detail: Measure light output at a set distance with a power meter, adjust the driver if needed, and check eye-safety limits before packaging.

prerequisites.why: red and near-infrared LEDs are mass-produced for lighting and remote controls, so suitable emitters are cheap and widely available.
stable current is needed to keep wavelength and output from drifting as the LEDs warm up.
research suggests light is absorbed by mitochondrial components, but the exact dose–response and signalling pathways are still debated.
some trials show modest effects on pain, skin or recovery, but many are small or poorly controlled, so results are not yet conclusive.
limits for eye and skin exposure to bright light guide safe design, though consumer panels vary in how strictly they follow them.

pathway.milestone: consumer panels sold for wellness and recovery with widely varying power and instructions
pathway.unlocks: low-cost access to red and near-infrared light at home.

pathway.milestone: standardised reporting of wavelength, irradiance and dose on every device
pathway.unlocks: users and researchers can compare devices and reproduce studies.

pathway.milestone: larger sham-controlled trials for specific conditions such as wound healing or joint pain
pathway.unlocks: clear evidence for which uses actually work and at what dose.

pathway.milestone: regulated medical devices with proven indications and optimised treatment protocols
pathway.unlocks: routine clinical use alongside or instead of existing therapies.
